label: Simple present tense
description: Base verb form for habitual actions, facts, and permanent states.
examples: I go to school every day.
She works at a hospital.
Water boils at 100°C.

label: Present continuous
description: be + -ing for actions happening now or temporary situations.
examples: I am reading a book.
She is working right now.

label: Simple past (regular verbs)
description: Completed past actions using the -ed ending.
examples: I walked to school.
She played tennis yesterday.

label: Simple past (irregular verbs)
description: Completed past actions using common irregular past forms.
examples: I went to the store.
She said goodbye.

label: Basic articles (a, an, the)
description: Indefinite (a/an) and definite (the) articles before nouns.
examples: I have a dog.
She is the teacher.
He ate an apple.

label: Subject pronouns
description: I, you, he, she, it, we, they as the subject of a clause.
examples: I am happy.
They go to school.
She is a doctor.

label: Imperative form
description: Commands and instructions using the bare infinitive.
examples: Open your book.
Don't move!
Please sit down.

label: Past continuous
description: was/were + -ing for actions in progress at a specific past time.
examples: I was reading when she called.
They were sleeping at midnight.

label: Present perfect (simple)
description: have/has + past participle for past actions with present relevance.
examples: I have finished my homework.
She has never seen snow.

label: Going to (future plans)
description: be going to for intentions, plans, and predictions based on evidence.
examples: I am going to study tomorrow.
She is going to have a baby.

label: Will (predictions and decisions)
description: will + infinitive for spontaneous decisions, promises, and predictions.
examples: I will help you.
It will rain tomorrow.
She won't forget.

label: Comparatives
description: Comparing two things: adjective + -er + than, or more + adjective + than.
examples: She is taller than me.
This is more expensive than that.

label: Superlatives
description: Highest or lowest degree: the + adjective + -est, or the most/least + adjective.
examples: She is the tallest in the class.
This is the most expensive option.

label: Modal verbs: can, must, should
description: Modal auxiliaries for ability (can), obligation (must), and advice (should).
examples: I can swim.
You must do your homework.
You should rest more.

label: Present perfect continuous
description: have/has been + -ing for actions started in the past and still ongoing.
examples: I have been studying all day.
She has been working here for five years.

label: Past perfect (simple)
description: had + past participle for actions completed before another past event.
examples: She had left before I arrived.
By noon he had finished the report.

label: Passive voice (present and past)
description: is/are/was/were + past participle to focus on the action rather than the agent.
examples: The letter was written yesterday.
The results are published online.

label: Defining relative clauses (who/which/that)
description: Clauses that identify which person or thing without commas.
examples: The man who called is my uncle.
The book that she wrote is famous.

label: First conditional (real possibility)
description: If + present simple → will + infinitive for likely future conditions.
examples: If it rains, I will stay home.
If you study hard, you will pass.

label: Gerunds and infinitives (verb patterns)
description: Verbs followed by -ing gerund or to-infinitive depending on the pattern.
examples: I enjoy swimming.
She decided to leave early.
He considered changing jobs.

label: Reported speech
description: Reporting what someone said with backshifted tenses after say/tell/ask.
examples: She said that she was tired.
He told me he had finished.
She asked if I was ready.

label: Modal verbs: might, may, could (possibility)
description: Expressing possibility and uncertainty in present or future situations.
examples: She might come tomorrow.
It may rain this evening.
That could be the answer.

label: Second conditional (hypothetical present/future)
description: If + past simple → would + infinitive for unlikely or imaginary conditions.
examples: If I had more time, I would travel more.
She would be happier if she changed jobs.

label: Third conditional (unreal past)
description: If + past perfect → would have + past participle for unreal past conditions.
examples: If she had studied, she would have passed.
He would have come if he had known.

label: Passive voice (extended tenses)
description: Passive constructions in future, perfect, and modal tenses.
examples: The project will be completed tomorrow.
The decision has been made.
Mistakes should be corrected immediately.

label: Cleft sentences for emphasis
description: It is/was + focus element + that/who to highlight part of a sentence.
examples: It was John who called.
It is the price that matters most.

label: Modal perfect (must have, should have)
description: Modal + have + past participle for deductions and regrets about past situations.
examples: She must have left already.
You should have told me.
He can't have forgotten.

label: Non-defining relative clauses
description: Extra information about a noun set off by commas using who/which/whose.
examples: My sister, who lives in London, is a doctor.
The film, which I saw last week, was excellent.

label: Concessive clauses (although, despite)
description: Contrasting ideas using although, even though, despite, in spite of.
examples: Although it was raining, we went out.
Despite being tired, she finished the project.

label: Inversion for emphasis (fronted negatives)
description: Subject-auxiliary inversion after negative/restrictive adverbs for formal emphasis.
examples: Never have I seen such beauty.
Rarely does she make mistakes.
Only then did he understand.

label: Participle clauses
description: Reduced adverbial clauses using present or past participles.
examples: Having finished the report, she left early.
Exhausted by the journey, he fell asleep.

label: Noun clauses (what-clauses, that-clauses)
description: Clauses functioning as noun phrases, often as subjects or objects.
examples: What she said surprised everyone.
The fact that he lied is unforgivable.
Whether or not you agree is irrelevant.

label: Complex reporting passives
description: Distancing structures: It is said to be, She is believed to have, etc.
examples: She is said to be the best candidate.
He was believed to have left the country.

label: Advanced conditionals with inversion
description: Formal conditionals omitting if and using subject-auxiliary inversion.
examples: Were she to leave, we would miss her greatly.
Had he known, he would have acted differently.

label: Ellipsis and substitution
description: Avoiding repetition by omitting elements (ellipsis) or using do so/one (substitution).
examples: She enjoys painting, and so do I.
If you need a pen, I have one.
He said he would help, and he did so.

label: Absolute constructions
description: Participial or nominal phrases grammatically independent from the main clause.
examples: The weather permitting, we will proceed.
All things considered, it was a great success.
That aside, the project was well managed.

label: Subjunctive mood (formal)
description: Bare infinitive in that-clauses after demand/suggest/recommend in formal registers.
examples: I suggest that he be given more time.
The committee recommends that funding be increased.
Were it not for her help, we would have failed.

label: Binomial and multinomial expressions
description: Fixed pairs and idioms with two or more elements in an established order.
markers: \b(by and large|all in all|to and fro|now and then|on and off|give and take|pros and cons|by and by)\b
examples: By and large, the project was a success.
They worked on and off throughout the year.
All in all, it was a worthwhile experience.

label: Fronting for emphasis
description: Moving a non-subject element to initial position for stylistic or emphatic effect.
examples: Brilliant though she is, she still has much to learn.
Strange as it may seem, he preferred silence.
This decision, I believe, will change everything.
